column5: fear of YHWH's word and protective action
column6: In the Moses-and-Pharaoh plague setting explicitly developed in the commentary, officials who fear YHWH's word act on the warning and bring servants and livestock under cover; reverent fear makes a transmitted warning beneficial.

The paired Pharaoh-scene verse describes the person who does not set his heart on YHWH's word and leaves those in his charge exposed, a concrete counterpart to the bedbaht recipient who keeps the reminder at a distance.

column5: Pharaoh's not knowing and not listening
column6: Pharaoh answers Moses that he does not know YHWH and will not listen to his voice; it binds failed knowledge to refusal of the prophetic command, beside the commentary's offer of guidance intended to yield fear.

column5: heart that fears and obedience for good
column6: YHWH wishes Israel had a heart to fear him and keep his commands so that it would go well with them; this joins reverential fear, reception of instruction, and benefit in one appeal.
At Horeb the people are gathered to hear God's words, learn to fear him, and teach their children, giving a communal scriptural form to the commentary's reminder that passes from speaker to hearer.

column5: public Torah reading, hearing, fear, observance
column6: The commanded assembly is to hear, learn, fear YHWH, and observe Torah; its ordered response closely matches instruction received by one who fears.

column5: teacher's address and fear of YHWH
column6: Come, children, listen to me; I will teach you the fear of YHWH makes fear the explicit subject of a directed instruction, rather than an undifferentiated emotion.

column5: reproof received by wise, hated by scoffer
column6: The proverb differentiates the recipient of reproof: the scoffer hates correction while the wise person loves it, a compact analogue to reminder received by one person and avoided by another.

column5: fear of YHWH and knowledge of God
column6: This verse places understanding the fear of YHWH alongside finding knowledge of God, supplying a Wisdom counterpart to the commentary's close account of fear and knowledge.

column5: hating knowledge and not choosing fear
column6: The rejected way is specified as both hatred of knowledge and refusal to choose the fear of YHWH, a precise negative counterpart to the fearful rememberer.
Isaiah identifies the person who trembles at God's word; the bodily image and reverent reception give a close counterpart to the commentary's "içi titreyen" hearer.

column5: teaching for benefit and leading in the way
column6: YHWH describes himself as the one who teaches Israel for its benefit and leads it in the way it should go, joining the commentary's benefit of reminder to its secondary guidance language.
The gentle speech commanded to Moses and Aaron in the commentary has a Wisdom analogue in the soft answer that turns away wrath; both treat the manner of address as consequential.
The command to rebuke one's neighbour makes correction an act directed toward another person, matching the commentary's insistence that reminder is transitive rather than merely inward recollection.

column5: hear or refuse a prophetic word
column6: Ezekiel is told to announce that whoever hears may hear and whoever refuses may refuse; the prophet delivers a word while the hearer divides into the two responses foregrounded here.

column5: warning, turning, and the watchman's limit
column6: If the watchman warns the wicked to turn, the warned person's response determines the outcome while the watchman has discharged his task; this illuminates both beneficial reminder and the commentary's limit on the reminder-giver.

column5: turning the shoulder and stopping the ears
column6: Those addressed refuse attention, turn a stubborn shoulder, and stop their ears from hearing; its physical language of withdrawal closely specifies the commentary's claim that the wretched person keeps admonition away rather than simply arguing with it.

Hebrew zkr is cognate with the source commentary's Arabic dhikr root. Joseph asks the cupbearer both to remember him and to cause Pharaoh to remember him, an especially clear instance of remembrance deliberately carried to another.

The Bavli's maxim that one should say a matter that will be heard and should not say one that will not be heard is a direct Jewish interpretive counterpart to the conditional "if the reminder benefits."

Hebrews says the word heard did not benefit its earlier hearers because it was not joined with faith, an unusually exact New Testament articulation of the commentary's conditional benefit of reminder.
Private reproof is directed to a brother, and hearing the reprover gains that brother; it concretely pairs transitive admonition with a beneficial response.
The community is to exhort one another daily so that none is hardened by sin's deceit; it makes repeated mutual reminder the antidote to the inward condition that refuses a divine word.

column5: Scripture profitable for teaching and reproof
column6: Scripture is called profitable for teaching, reproof, correction, and training, giving a direct Christian formulation of the reminder's possible usefulness.

The teacher corrects opponents with gentleness in hope that God grants repentance leading to knowledge of truth; this closely accompanies the commentary's gentle address to Pharaoh and its fear-knowledge nexus.
Those described turn their hearing away from the truth and turn aside to myths, a verbal and spatially shaped counterpart to the recipient who avoids the reminder.
James commands hearers to receive the implanted word, which is able to save them; its reception-versus-rejection logic makes the benefit of a delivered word explicit.

column5: blessed hearers and keepers of God's word
column6: Jesus calls those who hear God's word and keep it blessed, supplying the positive happy pole beside the commentary's fearful receiver and its contrast with the most wretched.
The warning not to refuse the one who speaks preserves the commentary's agency distinction: a divine word is offered, and refusal is the hearer's perilous response.
The good-soil hearers hear the word, accept it, and bear fruit; this gives a concrete Gospel image for a reminder whose reception has beneficial effect.

The Hiphil azkir, "cause my name to be remembered," belongs to the Hebrew zkr cognate family of Arabic dhikr. Its cultic setting adds an external, name-centred form of caused remembrance, not a claim that the two rituals are identical.

column5: fearers and a book of zikkaron
column6: The verse couples those who fear YHWH with a written zikkaron, "remembrance," from the Hebrew cognate family of dhikr; it is a distinct divine memorial usage alongside the commentary's human-directed reminder.

Proverbs calls fear of YHWH the beginning of knowledge, whereas the commentary says its reverential fear commonly arises from knowledge. The differing order is the point of comparison, while both tightly link the two.
God promises to put his fear in the people's hearts so that they will not turn away from him. It reverses the commentary's sequence by making fear the force that keeps a recipient from withdrawal.

A priest affected by seminal emission may not eat holy things until clean. This supplies a Hebrew Bible ritual analogue to the commentary's postcoital distance claim, while the verse concerns holy food rather than mosque prayer.

Before Sinai's divine encounter the people are told not to approach a woman. It makes sexual abstention part of preparation for sacred approach, a related but not identical frame to the commentary's junub explanation.

column5: baal qeri and recitation of Shema
column6: The mishnah limits a man with a seminal emission to inward reflection on the Shema rather than its normal verbal recitation. It provides a Jewish liturgical analogue to the commentary's association of the postcoital state with distance from prayer, without equating their rules.

column5: happiness and keeping away from wicked counsel
column6: Psalm 1 calls happy the person who keeps away from wicked counsel. Its ethical allocation reverses the commentary's image: distance is good when the counsel is wicked, while keeping a beneficial reminder distant marks the wretched person.

column5: blindness, ethical care, and fear of God
column6: The prohibition against putting a stumbling block before the blind concludes with fear of God. It gives a Torah ethical setting for the commentary's blind, fearful visitor, though it is not the same incident.

Paul permits spouses temporary, agreed abstinence in order to devote themselves to prayer. This is a close Christian prayer-and-sexuality parallel, but frames abstention as voluntary and temporary rather than an automatic ritual bar.

column5: Jesus stops for a blind petitioner
column6: Jesus stops and has the blind Bartimaeus called to him. Beside the commentary's rebuke of a prophet who turned from a blind seeker, it offers a controlled comparison of a religious teacher's response to a blind petitioner, not the same story.

The evil-doer hates the light and does not come to it lest deeds be exposed. Its avoidance is more active than verbal contradiction, clarifying the commentary's spatial account of shunning admonition.

column5: attention to what was heard and drifting away
column6: Hebrews calls for closer attention to what has been heard lest hearers drift away; the nautical image supplies a concrete Christian counterpart to turning aside from a reminder.
